WHAT THIS DOES AND DOES NOT DO

Observes: Wi-Fi and Bluetooth metadata broadcast publicly by nearby hardware. Does not identify people or vehicles. Does not intercept traffic. Advertisement and beacon metadata only. Does not find a camera recording to an SD card. Only things actively broadcasting. Cannot give a bearing. One antenna gives distance estimates, not direction. No camera. No microphone. No network calls. No accounts.

Bluetooth trackers rotate their address every few minutes, so the address is useless as identity. Instead each advertisement is reduced to a signature: company ID, service UUIDs, payload shape, and the payload bytes that stay fixed across a key rotation. A signature is flagged only when it turns up at three or more spatially separated GPS fixes, with a real time gap between them, outside any place you have marked as known. The threshold is deliberately high. Two locations is usually a coincidence, and an alert that cries wolf gets ignored.

Nothing has met the threshold. This is the expected state. Correlation needs GPS fixes at several separate places over time, so a session that has not moved will never produce an alert no matter what is nearby.
This is a correlation, not an identification. Check whether it belongs to you or someone you were with before treating it as anything else.
That device is no longer in the log.
Not enough sightings yet to draw a trace.
RSSI over time, fixed -100 to -20 dBm scale. Movement here is as often multipath or body shadowing as it is real distance change.
No sighting of this device carried a GPS fix, so it cannot contribute to correlation.
Below 30s, Android will refuse most of these requests and serve cached results instead. Turn off "Wi-Fi scan throttling" in Developer Options to make it real.
Correlation is suppressed inside a known place. Without this, a tracker in your own home flags itself every day and you stop reading the alerts.
Everything runs on-device. No network calls, no telemetry, no accounts. Vendor names come from a bundled copy of the public IEEE OUI registry.

A passive observer of the radio environment around you. It logs Wi-Fi and Bluetooth broadcasts over time, names the manufacturer behind an address where it can, and warns you if a Bluetooth beacon appears to be following you between places. Everything happens on this device.

It cannot find a camera recording to an SD card. Only things actively broadcasting appear. It cannot identify people or vehicles. It does not intercept traffic - advertisement and beacon metadata only. It cannot tell you which direction something is in. One antenna gives a rough distance, never a bearing. Vendor labels describe a manufacturer, not who owns a device or what it is being used for.

Android ties every scan result to the location permission. Without it, the system returns an empty list and there is nothing to show at all. That is a platform rule, not a choice this app made. Location is also what makes the tracker correlator work: deciding whether a beacon has followed you means knowing you were in different places. Your position is written to the local log and nowhere else.

No network permission is requested. No telemetry, no accounts, no cloud. The debrief export is plain text. If you want a model to read it, you paste it yourself - the app never sends anything anywhere.
No location fix yet. Wait for GPS and try again.
Correlation complete. Nothing met the threshold.
Machine-readable snapshots. Timestamps are UTC epoch milliseconds alongside ISO-8601, so a file still means something a year from now.

A plain-text summary of the environment: totals, density, band spread, category breakdown, notable hardware, and the limits of the method. Written to be pasted into a language model of your choosing, or read as-is.
